claims.text: A physics-informed machine-learning framework calibrated using mesoscale FEM can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness of HfNbTiVAl10 within 10–15% of experimental values.
The hybrid framework can reduce prediction time by approximately 50–60% relative to established full-scale simulations.
The HfNbTiVAl10 material has a hierarchical heterostructure with known grain-size distributions, phase interfaces, and pre-existing defect populations established by TEM/SEM.
Short-range-order metrics are available for the HfNbTiVAl10 material.
Grain boundaries, phase interfaces, and defect distributions mediate local stress localization in the hierarchical material.
Grain boundaries, phase interfaces, and defect distributions mediate local dislocation activity.
Mesoscale FEM incorporating explicit microstructural descriptors can capture key local stress events.
Mesoscale FEM incorporating dislocation-nucleation thresholds can capture key dislocation-nucleation events.
Training on FEM outputs and experimental results enables the machine-learning model to learn correlations between heterostructural descriptors and mechanical properties.
The learned correlations permit rapid mechanical-property prediction without full-scale atomistic computation.
Traditional full-scale atomistic simulations and unaugmented FEM models require longer computation times than the proposed hybrid framework.
Unaugmented FEM models may represent heterogeneous microstructural effects less accurately than the proposed framework.
The approach may fail when local plasticity and dislocation events deviate substantially from the calibrated thresholds.
Poor characterization of grain boundaries or defect densities can undermine calibration of the machine-learning model.
Dislocation nucleation occurring below the resolution of mesoscale FEM can undermine model calibration.
Literature on similar high-entropy alloys suggests that the proposed approach could improve predictive accuracy and computational efficiency.
